title: Being John Malkovich
full_review:
The ability to get inside the head of a celebrity is the unlikely premise of the surreal fantasy, ``Being John Malkovich'' (USA Films). The story opens with unemployed puppeteer Craig (John Cusack) taking a job as file clerk for a company run by a dotty old man (Orson Bean).

 

Located between the seventh and eighth floors of an office building, the rooms have such low ceilings that people have to crouch to make their way around. Bent over his work in the file room, Craig spots a tiny door hidden behind a cabinet which opens into a tunnel which sucks him into the mind of actor John Malkovich (playing himself), then spews him out alongside the New Jersey Turnpike.

Going right along with the fantasy premise is Maxine (Catherine Keener), Craig's self-centered co- worker, who opens the tunnel to those willing to pay for 15 minutes with a celebrity.

Directed by Spike Jonze from a script by Charlie Kaufman, the odd proceedings grow progressively more bizarre as Maxine becomes sexually attracted to Craig's wife (Cameron Diaz) while making loving to Malkovich. The weird triangle grows to include Craig after he gradually takes control of Malkovich's body as well as his mind, then marries Maxine and achieves success as a puppeteer until his doddering old boss wants to switch bodies with the actor. The wit and imagination used to set up the strange situation get lost in endless complications that grow tiresomely unamusing long before the ending's final twist.

Because of several sexual encounters, many sexual references, some rough language and occasional profanity, The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling.The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
